items.question: How far behind its rivals is Northstar with Gen Z? Give Northstar's aided awareness among Gen Z, Vantage Athletic's FY2025 revenue scale, and the share of Pace & Co.'s active customers who are Gen Z.

args.query: Northstar aided awareness among Gen Z
Vantage Athletic FY2025 revenue
Pace & Co. active customers Gen Z share
Northstar Gen Z aided awareness percent 46%

items.content:
### Answer

Northstar's aided awareness among Gen Z is 46%, against 71% for Vantage Athletic, a gap the Q3 review puts at 25 points [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL6]]. Vantage Athletic is far larger, with FY2025 net revenue of about $4.2 billion [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-DECK@v1:SL3]]. Gen Z customers account for 44% of Pace & Co.'s active customer file [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B4]].

### Key findings

- Northstar's aided brand awareness among Gen Z consumers stands at 46%, versus 71% for Vantage Athletic [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]]; Vantage's own investor deck also cites 71% [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-DECK@v1:SL10]].
- Vantage Athletic's FY2025 net revenue was $4.2 billion, with footwear at 63% of sales [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-DECK@v1:SL3]]. The Northstar strategy document says "about $4.2 billion" [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B2]].
- Northstar's net revenue is on track to grow from $571.0 million in FY25 to a latest estimate of $612.0 million in FY26 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]].
- Gen Z customers account for 44% of Pace & Co.'s active customer file; Pace has expanded store-in-store doors from 640 to 1,100 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B4]].
- Northstar's Gen Z share of net revenue was 21% in FY25, with a board target of 30% by the end of FY28 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]].

### Conflicting evidence

- E3 sets an interim goal of closing "at least ten points of the gap to Vantage Athletic" by the end of FY27, while E9 states the gap as 25 points [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P7.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL6]]. These are consistent with each other (a goal versus the current gap). I found no conflicting values for the three requested metrics.
- E3 also indicates that a reconciled Gen Z definition will be published for board use, which suggests Gen Z-related figures may be restated [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P7.B2]]. E10 likewise notes that Gen Z definitions differ between teams [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P7.B1]].

### Interpretation

Northstar trails Vantage on awareness by a wide margin and is a fraction of its revenue scale, but Pace & Co. is a different kind of rival, with a customer base heavily weighted toward Gen Z [inference]. Comparing Pace's 44% Gen Z customer-file share with Northstar's 21% revenue share is not like-for-like, since the two metrics measure different things [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence gives no Gen Z awareness figure for Pace & Co., and no Gen Z share of Vantage Athletic's revenue or customers [inference]. Northstar's Gen Z share of its active customer file is not stated on the same basis as Pace's metric. Pace & Co.'s total revenue is also not given. Competitor disclosures or a brand-tracker cut covering all three brands on a common Gen Z definition would close these gaps.

items.question: Size up the social-commerce opportunity: what share of Gen Z athletic footwear purchases now happen on social platforms according to the latest trend panel, how fast did Northstar's Social Shop grow quarter over quarter in Q2 FY26, and how big is the FY27 Gen Z marketing budget the strategy team proposes?

args.query: share of Gen Z athletic footwear purchases on social platforms trend panel
Northstar Social Shop quarter over quarter growth Q2 FY26
FY27 Gen Z marketing budget proposal strategy team
Social Shop revenue grew % versus Q1 channel momentum

items.content:
### Answer

According to the 2026 trends panel, social commerce platforms account for 26% of Gen Z athletic footwear purchases [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]]. Northstar's Social Shop sales grew 142% quarter over quarter in Q2 FY26, the fastest of any channel [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL5]]. The strategy team proposes a FY27 Gen Z marketing budget of $24 million [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]].

### Key findings

- Social commerce platforms account for 26% of Gen Z athletic footwear purchases in the 2026 panel, with gains in every region and age band [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]].
- Social Shop sales grew 142% quarter over quarter, the fastest of any channel [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL5]].
- The proposed FY27 Gen Z marketing budget is $24 million, of which 40% would shift to creator and community programs [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]].
- The allocation includes $9.6 million for creator and community programs and $5.4 million for Social Shop and performance channels [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]].
- Social checkout converts better than brand sites for impulse categories, but return rates on social orders are also higher [[NORTHSTAR/ANALYST-CALL@v1:S1.B2]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The 26% figure is from the 2026 panel [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]]. The panel analyst said the panel's social measurement will be restated upward in the next edition, because earlier panels undercounted young shoppers [[NORTHSTAR/ANALYST-CALL@v1:S1.B2]]. The 26% may therefore be understated.

### Interpretation

Social is already a sizeable and fast-growing route to market, but the 142% growth rate should not be read as a measure of scale given the small starting base [inference]. The proposed budget shift toward creators and Social Shop is consistent with the channel's momentum, though higher return rates and service constraints could erode the economics [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not give Social Shop's absolute revenue or its share of Northstar's Gen Z sales, so the real size of the opportunity is unclear. The restated panel figure is not yet available. Return-rate and service-cost data for Social Shop orders would be needed to assess profitability [inference]. A published channel-level P&L would close these gaps.

items.question: Put Northstar's numbers in market context: its FY26 latest-estimate net revenue, the growth expected from Gen Z revenue in FY26, and the size of the 2026 US Gen Z athletic footwear market.

args.query: Northstar FY26 latest estimate net revenue
Gen Z revenue growth FY26 Northstar
2026 US Gen Z athletic footwear market size

items.content:
### Answer

Northstar's FY26 latest-estimate net revenue is $612.0 million [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B3]][[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL3]]. Gen Z revenue is projected to grow 13.8% in FY26, about double the company's overall growth [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P2.B1]][[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]]. The 2026 US Gen Z athletic footwear market is estimated at 18.6 $bn, growing 6.9% year over year [[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R5]]. Gen Z revenue is therefore projected to grow faster than that market [inference].

### Key findings

- FY26 latest-estimate net revenue is $612.0 million, up from $571.0 million in FY25, growth of roughly 7% [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B3]].
- Gen Z (18-27) revenue is projected at 126.1 $m in FY26, up from 110.8 $m in FY25, with yoy growth of 13.8% [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]][[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P2.B1]].
- The 2026 US Gen Z athletic footwear market is 18.6 $bn (estimate), with yoy_growth_pct of 6.9 [[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R5]]. The 2025 figure was 17.4 $bn with 7.4% growth [[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R4]].
- The adjacent personalized athletic footwear niche is 1.1 $bn in 2026, with yoy_growth_pct of 22.2 [[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R17]].

### Conflicting evidence

- Gen Z share of revenue: the finance definition (ages 18 to 27) gives 19.4% for FY25 [[NORTHSTAR/FIN-SUMMARY-FY26@v1:SH2.R2]], while the executive summary cites 21% for FY25 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]]. The difference stems from the brand team's wider 16-29 age band [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P2.B1]].
- The evidence notes flag differing "year" values across market sizing rows [[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R17]][[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R5]][[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R16]][[NORTHSTAR/CATEGORY-SIZING@v1:SH1.R4]]. These are rows for different years (2025 and 2026), not contradictory values for the same metric.

### Interpretation

Because the 13.8% Gen Z revenue growth exceeds the 6.9% market growth, Northstar appears to be gaining share within the Gen Z footwear market, though the revenue figure covers all categories, not footwear alone [inference]. The two figures are not like-for-like, so the comparison is directional only [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not break out Northstar's Gen Z footwear revenue, so its actual share of the Gen Z footwear market cannot be established. Finance reporting by category within the Gen Z segment would close this. FY26 figures are latest estimates because the year is not closed, and the market figures are modeled estimates from a third party [inference]. The market and finance Gen Z definitions may differ in age range, which limits comparability. A documented definition from the market-sizing source would help [inference].

items.question: Survey respondent R0388 named a premium they would accept. What was it and what condition did they attach, and how does stated acceptance in the external willingness-to-pay study change at a 25% premium?

args.query: willingness to pay study acceptance at 25% price premium

items.content:
### Answer

Respondent R0388 said they would pay about 15% more for shoes made to their foot, but only if the shoes arrive as fast as normal ones [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R389]]. In the external study, stated acceptance among Gen Z falls steeply at a 25% premium: only 12% accepted it, versus 38% at a 15% fit premium [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B2]].

### Key findings

- R0388's verbatim: "maybe 15% more, but only if they arrive as fast as normal ones" [[NORTHSTAR/SURVEY-2026@v1:R389]].
- 38% of Gen Z respondents would pay a 15% premium for fit-personalized footwear [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B2]].
- Only 12% of Gen Z respondents accepted a 25% premium [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B2]].
- The study describes the drop as steep above 15%, with offers beyond that point treated as a luxury [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B2]].
- The study's price range ran up to a 25% premium in five steps [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B1]].
- The study stresses its percentages are stated measures and should be treated as a ceiling, not a sales forecast [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P4.B1]].

### Gaps & unknowns

It does not establish how many other Northstar respondents attach the same delivery condition [inference]. Pilot or order data with real prices would show whether stated acceptance converts to purchases [inference].

items.question: SKU NS-KR2: what is its FY26 return rate, and what were customers contacting support about for that shoe in Q3, and in what volume?

args.query: Knit Runner 2 support contacts Q3 themes volume
Knit Runner 2 FY26 return rate

items.content:
### Answer

The Knit Runner 2 has a stated return rate of 16.8%, compared with 13.1% for the original Knit Runner [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL8]]. In Q3, customers contacted support mainly about knit upper wear, specifically fraying near the toe flex point, which rose to 1,140 tickets [[NORTHSTAR/SUPPORT-THEMES@v1:P2.B2]]. The evidence gives the return rate without an explicit FY26 label, and it does not map the product name to the SKU code NS-KR2 in any retrievable row [[NORTHSTAR/PRODUCT-PERF@v1:SH3.T1]][[NORTHSTAR/PRODUCT-PERF@v1:SH2.T1]].

### Key findings

- Return rate on the Knit Runner 2 is 16.8%, against 13.1% for the original Knit Runner [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL8]]. The brand strategy document repeats the same two figures [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P6.B3]].
- Complaints about knit upper wear on the Knit Runner 2 rose to 1,140 tickets in Q3, most citing fraying near the toe flex point within 90 days [[NORTHSTAR/SUPPORT-THEMES@v1:P2.B2]].
- Ticket volume understates the problem, because returns data show a larger number of durability returns that never generated a contact [[NORTHSTAR/SUPPORT-THEMES@v1:P2.B2]].
- Before September, frontline guidance classified early fraying as normal wear unless a manufacturing defect could be shown; guidance changed in late September to treat early toe fraying as a product issue eligible for replacement or refund [[NORTHSTAR/SUPPORT-THEMES@v1:P2.B2]].
- A representative customer note describes toe fraying in under three months, an agent calling it normal wear, and the customer switching brands [[NORTHSTAR/SUPPORT-THEMES@v1:P3.B4]].

### Interpretation

The pre-September guidance may have inflated repeat contacts, so the ticket count may partly reflect handling rather than only new defects [[NORTHSTAR/SUPPORT-THEMES@v1:P2.B2]] [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The number of durability returns without contacts is not quantified; the Returns sheet rows for this SKU would provide it [inference].

items.question: One interviewee says their last three pairs came from a run club group chat rather than ads. How does Vantage Athletic's stated mission and homepage emphasis compare with that discovery route?

args.query: Vantage Athletic mission statement and homepage messaging
last three pairs came from run club group chat, not ads

items.content:
### Answer

Vantage Athletic's stated mission and homepage emphasis centre on performance and race results, not on community or peer discovery [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B3]][[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B2]]. The interviewee found their last three pairs through a run club group chat rather than ads [[NORTHSTAR/INTERVIEWS@v1:S13.Q1]]. The evidence shows no Vantage content that addresses group-chat or word-of-mouth discovery, so the two are largely misaligned in emphasis, though the evidence does not show how Vantage actually acquires customers [inference].

### Key findings

- Vantage describes its mission as "engineering speed for athletes who compete," and its homepage leads with race results rather than lifestyle imagery [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B3]].
- The hero copy is "Built for the finish line" and stresses stopwatch, wear tests and athletes who will not compromise [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B2]].
- Vantage marketing leads with finish line results, and the homepage is organised the same way [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-DECK@v1:SL6.N1]].
- The interviewee says "Ads wash right over me," but a friend's report of a shoe working on a long run gets their attention [[NORTHSTAR/INTERVIEWS@v1:S13.Q1]].
- Gen Z focus group participants rely on people they know or follow, and some said the group chat was the first place they heard about a new product [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B7]].
- Another source names run clubs, campus teams, studio classes and group chats as the most trusted discovery routes [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B4]].
- Vantage does offer team pricing for collegiate and club programmes, and a membership giving individual athletes early access to race releases [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B13]].

### Interpretation

Vantage's results-led messaging is a brand-side broadcast approach, whereas the interviewee's route is peer-to-peer, so the homepage is unlikely to be the main trigger for this kind of buyer [inference]. The club team pricing programme could be a partial bridge to community channels, but nothing in the evidence shows it is used for discovery [inference]. Performance credentials could still matter once a friend recommends a shoe, but the evidence does not test this [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not show how Vantage actually acquires customers, whether it runs community, club or creator programmes beyond team pricing, or how its advertising performs. It also covers a single interviewee and a small focus group, so it cannot indicate how widespread this discovery route is among Vantage's target buyers [inference]. Vantage channel-mix or marketing-spend data, and a survey of its own customers' discovery sources, would close these gaps.

items.question: What kind of personalization got the Gen Z focus-group participants most excited, and how does Vantage Athletic's personalization offer compare with that?

args.query: Gen Z focus group personalization excited
Vantage Athletic personalization offer
Vantage Fit Lab gait scanning personalization fit

items.content:
### Answer

Focus-group participants reacted most strongly to personalization framed as a status signal that friends would notice, such as initials on a heel tab, a team or club colorway, or a limited release few friends would own [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]]. Vantage's offer is narrower: a choice of 12 preset colorways on its flagship racer only [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B4]]. It overlaps with the colorway-style excitement but offers no initials or stitched names, and no personalization beyond that one shoe [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B4]].

### Key findings

- The stimulus round generated the most energy of the session, and participants lit up at a stitched name, a club colorway, or a limited release only a few friends would own [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]].
- Several participants said they would post a picture of a personalized pair before a standard one [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]].
- Vantage offers personalization "only as a choice of 12 preset colorways on its flagship racer" [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B4]]; Brand Strategy likewise describes it as limited to 12 preset colorways [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B2]].
- Vantage keeps the engineering identical for every runner so a custom tweak does not undo the tuning of plate, foam and geometry [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B4]].
- Vantage's Fit Lab recommends from the existing range and the company has no plans for made-to-order manufacturing [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-WEB@v1:S1.B7]][[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-DECK@v1:SL8.N1]].

### Interpretation

Vantage's preset colorways partly match the "club colorway" appeal, but they are chosen from a fixed list rather than being personal marks like initials or a name [inference]. Vantage's offer is a product-configuration choice and Fit Lab is a fit service, so neither delivers the individual status signal that excited participants [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The focus group had ten participants and reflects stated reactions in a hypothetical setting, so it cannot show how many Gen Z shoppers share this excitement [inference]. The evidence does not show how Gen Z shoppers view Vantage's colorway offer specifically, since the group was not shown it. Reactions to Vantage's actual offer would require a customer test or survey. The evidence does not say whether Vantage plans to extend its personalization beyond the flagship racer.

items.question: What made a shopper who loved the custom colorway tool give up on ordering, and what did Northstar leadership decide about personalization at the Q3 strategy review?

args.query: shopper loved custom colorway tool but abandoned order
Northstar Q3 strategy review decision personalization

items.content:
### Answer

A shopper who loved the custom colorway tool gave up on ordering because of the twelve day wait [[NORTHSTAR/INTERVIEWS@v1:S14.Q1]]. At the Q3 strategy review, leadership agreed to pause any national rollout of personalization until the full pilot readout in October, and the decision requested was to hold it at a limited test [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL14.N1]][[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL14]].

### Key findings

- Interview 12 (Sam K.) said he "loved" the custom colorway tool, but "the twelve day wait killed it for me" [[NORTHSTAR/INTERVIEWS@v1:S14.Q1]].
- Sam K. said that if the order had come in a few days, he "would have bought two pairs" [[NORTHSTAR/INTERVIEWS@v1:S14.Q1]].
- Other pilot-related feedback also points to waiting time as a barrier: one interviewee loved the online colorway tool but abandoned the order after seeing the wait [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B8]].
- Leadership agreed to pause any national rollout of personalization until the full pilot readout in October [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL14.N1]].
- The stated reasoning was that the early signal came from a tiny sample and the operational constraints are significant [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL14.N1]].
- The Q3 review's first decision requested was to "Hold personalization at a limited test and defer any national rollout decision" [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL14]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The Q3 review's reasoning cites an early signal from a tiny sample [[NORTHSTAR/Q3-REVIEW@v1:SL14.N1]]. The pilot final readout says an early read circulated in July suggested a more favorable picture, but it was based on week six data and a very small sample and "should be treated as superseded" [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B2]].
- The final readout states the evidence does not support the hypothesis that young customers will pay a premium for made-for-them products, in the form tested [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B2]]. It recommends keeping personalization as a limited test.

### Interpretation

The pause and limited-test decision rests on the earlier, smaller read, while the later final readout reaches a more negative conclusion on the premium hypothesis yet recommends the same limited-test posture [inference]. The shopper's reason for abandoning (delivery wait) is consistent with the wait being the main reason given by pilot customers for not returning [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B2]] [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not show whether leadership formally confirmed each requested decision at the meeting, only that the pause was agreed and the hold was requested. It also does not say whether the October full readout has changed the decision [inference]. A post-October leadership record or decision log would close this gap.

items.question: Customers say they discover shoes through run clubs and group chats rather than ads. How large is the proposed FY27 Gen Z marketing budget, and how much of it would move toward creator and community programmes?

args.query: FY27 Gen Z marketing budget creator and community programmes
discover shoes through run clubs and group chats rather than ads

items.content:
### Answer

The proposed FY27 Gen Z marketing budget is $24 million, of which 40% would shift to creator and community programs [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]]. The memo allocates $9.6 million to creator and community programs [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]]. The customer evidence is consistent with this direction, since interviewees and focus group participants say they learn about shoes through run clubs, group chats and creators rather than ads [[NORTHSTAR/INTERVIEWS@v1:S13.Q1]][[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B7]].

### Key findings

- Proposed FY27 Gen Z marketing budget: $24 million, with 40% shifting to creator and community programs [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]].
- Creator and community programs are allocated $9.6 million; other lines are $5.4 million for Social Shop and performance channels, $4.5 million for Fit Promise launch and fit education content, $3.0 million for brand and awareness building, and $1.5 million for measurement and test reserve [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]].
- The shift is funded mainly by reducing broad reach advertising and trimming spend on promotions that discount core styles [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B7]].
- One interviewee found his last three pairs through a run club group chat, not ads [[NORTHSTAR/INTERVIEWS@v1:S13.Q1]].
- Focus group participants named friends, team mates, class groups and creators as sources, and some said the group chat was the first place they heard about a new product [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B7]].
- The memo states that customers say they trust peer reviews and creator videos more than brand advertising [[NORTHSTAR/FY27-MEMO@v1:S1.B5]].

### Interpretation

The budget shift toward creators and community appears to be aimed at the discovery behaviour customers describe, though the evidence does not show the memo was designed specifically around run clubs or group chats [inference]. Run clubs and group chats are peer channels that brand-run creator and community programs may only partly reach, so the fit between the spend and this behaviour is not established [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

It does not say how much creator and community spend would go to run-club or group-chat style activity versus other creator programs [inference]. It also lacks evidence on the effectiveness or return of such spending, which would require pilot results or channel attribution data.

items.question: Northstar is sizing a paid fit-personalization tier at a 15% markup. What uptake should it plan for: the stated acceptance in the external study, or the take-up actually observed when pilot shoppers were offered that tier?

args.query: fit personalization paid tier 15% markup uptake pilot shoppers

items.content:
### Answer

Northstar should plan on the take-up observed in the pilot, which was 9% of shoppers choosing the 15% tier [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B5]][[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B12]], not the stated acceptance from the external study. The study reported roughly two in five Gen Z respondents saying they would pay about 15% more [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B9]], and its own authors advise treating those percentages as a ceiling, not a sales forecast [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P4.B1]]. Northstar's pilot readout recommends using revealed behaviour for any revenue assumption and stated willingness to pay only as a ceiling [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B9]].

### Key findings

- Only 9% of pilot shoppers selected the 15% premium tier for personalized fit, and most chose the free monogram [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B5]][[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B12]].
- The external study found roughly two in five Gen Z respondents saying they would pay about 15% more [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B9]].
- Pilot uptake was less than a quarter of the stated share, a larger gap than is typical even allowing for survey overstatement [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B9]].
- The study's authors say the gap between stated acceptance and observed uptake tends to be largest for attractive but non-essential features, and recommend treating percentages as a ceiling [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P4.B1]].
- Possible reasons for the gap include real money at point of sale, a 12 day lead time that was not part of the study scenario, and the free monogram alternative [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B9]][[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B12]].
- Customer survey verbatims say they would pay a bit more only if delivery were as fast as standard, a condition the pilot could not meet [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B9]].
- An outside analyst said low paid-tier uptake would be consistent with other clients he has seen [[NORTHSTAR/ANALYST-CALL@v1:S1.B2]].

### Conflicting evidence

- Stated side: roughly two in five Gen Z respondents said they would pay about 15% more [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B9]].
- Revealed side: 9% of pilot shoppers chose the 15% tier [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B5]][[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B12]].
- An early July read was more favorable but was based on week six data and a very small sample, and is superseded by the final results [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B12]].

### Interpretation

A planning base case near the observed 9% is better supported than the stated figure, since it reflects real prices and orders [inference]. Uptake could differ if lead time were cut to match standard delivery, but the evidence does not show by how much, so any upside should be treated as a scenario rather than the base case [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The pilot covered three stores plus online, so it may not represent a national rollout [inference]. No evidence shows uptake at a lower premium or with faster delivery. A repeat pilot with shorter lead time on a single style, or a test of different price points, would close these gaps.

items.question: Should Northstar lead its Gen Z messaging with personalization? Check what framing excited the focus group most, and where personalization landed when participants allocated a fixed budget of points across benefits.

args.query: Gen Z focus group personalization messaging framing excited participants
participants allocated points across benefits budget personalization ranking
focus group budget allocation points fit guarantees delivery speed materials personalization share

items.content:
### Answer

Personalization excited the focus group most when it was framed as a status signal that friends would notice [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]]. But when participants spent a hypothetical 100 points, it did not lead: fit guarantee, faster delivery and honest materials information ranked ahead of it [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]]. The evidence therefore does not support leading Gen Z messaging with personalization; it is better positioned as a gifting, team and status feature [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S4.B1]].

### Key findings

- The strongest reaction came from personalization framed as a status signal, such as initials on a heel tab or a team colorway; several participants said they would post a personalized pair before a standard one [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]].
- In the points allocation exercise, participants ranked fit guarantee, faster delivery and honest materials information ahead of personalization [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]].
- Participants described a shoe that fits and arrives quickly as something they need, and a personalized shoe as something they would enjoy [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]].
- The focus group's own implications recommend positioning personalization as a gifting, team and status feature tested in small steps, not as the lead reason to buy [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S4.B1]].
- Waiting was acceptable for gifts and special items, but longer lead times on everyday purchases were a reason to shop elsewhere [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B5]].
- Pilot feedback was consistent: customers liked the scan and colorway tool but complained about waiting time, and one reviewer said the order took almost two weeks and she nearly cancelled [[NORTHSTAR/PERSO-PILOT@v1:S1.B8]].
- A separate willingness-to-pay study found longer waits reduced acceptance of a premium at every price level [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P3.B2]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The willingness-to-pay study scores personalized fit at 45% relative importance, the top attribute, versus 15% for personalized colorway and 7% for name or initials [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P3.B2]]. The focus group put personalization behind fit guarantees and other basics [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-FOCUS-GROUP@v1:S3.B6]]. These measure different things (a conjoint on personalization options versus a point allocation across benefits), so they may be compatible: fit-based personalization appears more valued than cosmetic personalization.

### Interpretation

The most defensible lead message for Gen Z is fit confidence and delivery reliability, with personalization as a secondary, delight-oriented layer [inference]. If personalization is highlighted, fit-based personalization appears the stronger angle, while cosmetic options such as initials carry less weight [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The focus group had only ten participants, and its allocation exercise reflects stated priorities in a hypothetical setting, so the ranking is directional, not statistical [inference]. The evidence does not show how personalization-led messaging would perform with real customers, in tests of ads or landing pages, or whether Gen Z survey data confirm the focus group ranking. A messaging A/B test and the survey data on stated priorities would close these gaps.

items.question: How many people did the external willingness-to-pay study survey, and how did the older millennial respondents compare on paying a 15% premium for fit-personalized shoes?

args.query: willingness-to-pay study 15% premium fit-personalized shoes older millennials survey respondents

items.content:
### Answer

The study surveyed 2,400 US consumers aged 16 to 40 in March 2026 [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P1.B3]]. Millennials were less willing to pay: 29% said they would pay a 15% premium for fit-personalized footwear, versus 38% of Gen Z [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B3]][[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P3.B3]]. The evidence does not break out "older millennials" as a separate group [inference].

### Key findings

- The sample was 2,400 US consumers aged 16 to 40, including 1,350 Gen Z respondents and roughly 780 millennials [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P1.B3]].
- Among millennial respondents, 29% would accept a 15% premium for fit personalization [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B3]][[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P3.B3]].
- The comparable Gen Z figure is 38% [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P2.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P3.B3]].
- Margins of error for the Gen Z and millennial groups are roughly plus or minus three points [[NORTHSTAR/WTP-STUDY@v1:P1.B3]].

### Interpretation

The gap between the two cohorts (29% vs 38%) is larger than the stated margin of error, so it likely reflects a real difference in stated willingness to pay rather than noise [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence reports millennials as a single group and gives no age split within it, so a comparison specific to older millennials cannot be made [inference]. A cross-tab of the survey data by exact age band would close this gap.

items.question: How much of Gen Z athletic spending now flows through third-party platforms instead of brand-owned sites, and how far do young shoppers trust fellow customers over advertising?

args.query: Gen Z athletic apparel footwear spending share through third-party platforms marketplaces vs brand-owned direct sites
young consumers trust peer reviews and other customers more than advertising
share of Gen Z purchases on marketplaces or third-party retailers rather than brand sites percent

items.content:
### Answer

Marketplace and social commerce together took 34% of Gen Z athletic spend in 2026, versus 22% for brand owned sites [[NORTHSTAR/CHANNEL-SHIFT@v1:S1.B2]]. Separately, social commerce alone accounts for 26% of Gen Z athletic footwear purchases, though an analyst expects that figure to be restated upward [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/ANALYST-CALL@v1:S1.B2]]. On trust, 57% of Gen Z respondents said they trust peer reviews and creator try on videos more than brand advertising [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].

### Key findings

- Marketplace and social commerce together took 34% of Gen Z athletic spend in 2026, compared with 22% for brand owned sites [[NORTHSTAR/CHANNEL-SHIFT@v1:S1.B2]].
- Social commerce platforms account for 26% of Gen Z athletic footwear purchases, per the 2026 panel [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]].
- 57% of Gen Z respondents trust peer reviews and creator try on videos more than brand advertising [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Advertising was seen as a prompt to look, not a reason to buy, and reviews on fit, sizing and durability were rated most useful [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P4.B1]].
- Brand owned sites are losing share of first purchases [[NORTHSTAR/CHANNEL-SHIFT@v1:S1.B2]].
- An analyst reports that creator videos and peer reviews are the strongest purchase triggers, but return rates on social orders are also higher [[NORTHSTAR/ANALYST-CALL@v1:S1.B2]].

### Conflicting evidence

- The 26% social commerce figure comes from the 2026 panel [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]]. The analyst says the panel's measurement will be restated upward in its next edition because earlier panels undercounted young shoppers [[NORTHSTAR/ANALYST-CALL@v1:S1.B2]]. The 26% is therefore likely a floor, and no restated value is provided.
- The 34% figure covers all spend across marketplaces and social combined [[NORTHSTAR/CHANNEL-SHIFT@v1:S1.B2]], while the 26% covers footwear purchases through social alone [[NORTHSTAR/GENZ-TRENDS@v2:P2.B2]]. These measure different things and are not directly comparable.

### Interpretation

The 34% vs 22% comparison suggests third-party platforms now take a larger share of Gen Z athletic spend than brand owned sites, though the two figures come from a single note and may differ in scope from the footwear-only data [inference]. The trust finding helps explain the channel shift, since creator videos and reviews live on social and marketplace platforms rather than brand sites [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not give a single reconciled share of Gen Z spend through third-party platforms, nor a restated social commerce figure. A methodology note or the next edition of the trends report would close these gaps.

### Interpretation

The 2.3x figure indicates top-of-funnel interest in colorway customization, not demonstrated purchase demand [inference]. Because stated or click-based interest can overstate real behaviour, the uplift should be treated as a directional signal rather than a sales forecast [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not give absolute click-through rates, send volumes, test duration, audience segments or statistical significance. It does not establish downstream conversion, revenue per send, or whether the "standard creative" baseline matches the full set of regular sends [inference]. Closing these gaps would require the underlying email test report or campaign analytics, including conversion and order data.

items.question: What brand position does Northstar's 2026 brand strategy want to own with active Gen Z consumers?

args.query: Northstar 2026 brand strategy position to own with Gen Z active consumers
we want Northstar to be the brand known for; positioning statement; own the position
four pillars dependable fit honest materials built to last community first trusted brand for young athletes

items.content:
### Answer

Northstar intends to position itself as the dependable fit brand for active Gen Z consumers, rather than competing on elite performance claims [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]]. It will not out-engineer the premium incumbent or out-discount value players, and instead aims to win customers who want predictability and trust in the basics [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]][[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B6]].

### Key findings

- The stated recommendation is to be "the dependable fit brand for active Gen Z consumers" rather than compete on elite performance claims [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]].
- The strategy says customers do not reject Northstar for lacking elite performance credentials and do not primarily ask for customization; they ask for predictability [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B6]].
- Four pillars translate the position into daily decisions, starting with dependable fit: one sizing logic across footwear, bottoms, tops and outerwear, backed by a clear exchange promise [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B6]].
- The other pillars are honest materials (plain disclosure of recycled content and production locations), built to last (durability standards and fast, fair handling of early failures), and community first (programs led by clubs, studios and creators rather than broadcast advertising) [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P6.B1]].
- Performance and personalization stay part of the story but not its headline, and neither may distract from fixing the basics [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P6.B1]].
- The main obstacles cited are unpredictable sizing, doubt that price is justified by durability, and impatience with brands that cannot explain what products are made of [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]].
- The strategy links the position to the board target of lifting the Gen Z share of revenue to 30% by the end of FY28 [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P1.B2]].

### Interpretation

The position is a trust-based, "get the basics right" claim aimed at turning Gen Z customers who like the product into advocates, which fits the stated gap between Gen Z and older customers on recommendation [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P2.B2]] [inference].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence does not show how well this position is resonating with Gen Z customers today, since the KPIs meant to test it are not included here. It also does not detail how the pillars will be resourced or sequenced [inference].

items.question: What net revenue did Vantage Athletic report for FY2025?

args.query: Vantage Athletic FY2025 net revenue

items.content:
### Answer

Vantage Athletic reported FY2025 net revenue of $4.2 billion [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-DECK@v1:SL3]]. Northstar's brand strategy document gives the same figure, described as "about $4.2 billion" [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B2]].

### Key findings

- Vantage's own Investor Day deck states net revenue of $4.2 billion in FY2025, with footwear at 63% of sales [[NORTHSTAR/VANTAGE-DECK@v1:SL3]].
- Northstar's internal strategy document independently cites FY2025 net revenue of about $4.2 billion and the same 63% footwear share [[NORTHSTAR/BRAND-STRATEGY@v1:P5.B2]].

### Gaps & unknowns

The evidence gives only a rounded headline figure, not an exact reported value [inference]. The evidence note says some figures were restated or superseded, but it does not specify which ones, and nothing in the cited Vantage items indicates a restatement of this number [inference]. A Vantage annual report or filing would confirm the precise figure and any revisions [inference].
